paragraphs.heading: What a bed is
paragraphs.text: In geology, a bed is one layer of sediment, of sedimentary rock or of volcanic rock. It has a bedding surface above it and another below it, and these are more or less well defined. A bedding surface, or bedding plane, is what visibly separates one bed from the bed before or after it. The neighbouring beds may be of the same lithology or a different one.

paragraphs.heading: Bed or lamina
paragraphs.text: Sedimentologists define a bed in two main ways. In the first, thickness does not matter: a bed is any coherent layer bounded above and below by bedding planes, and laminae are small beds, the smallest visible layers. In the second, thickness decides: a coherent layer more than 1 cm thick is a bed, and one less than 1 cm thick is a lamina. Both definitions have merit, and which one is used depends on the focus of the study.

paragraphs.heading: What the surfaces record
paragraphs.text: Bedding surfaces typically, though not always, record a change in the rate or type of sediment that was accumulating. They usually stand for a time of no deposition, erosion that cut the bed off, a shift in flow or sediment regime, an abrupt change in composition, or some mix of these. For that reason a bed is typically read as a single period of time when material built up under uniform, steady conditions. Some bedding surfaces, though, may be features formed or enhanced after deposition, for example by weathering.

paragraphs.heading: Shapes and types of bed
paragraphs.text: Most often the top and bottom surfaces of a bed are parallel or nearly so. Some beds have surfaces that are not parallel, such as wavy or curved ones. Types of beds include cross-beds and graded beds. Cross-beds are not layered horizontally; they form through local deposition on the sloping surfaces of ripples or dunes, combined with local erosion. Graded beds show a gradual change in grain size from one side of the bed to the other. In normal grading the larger grains are on the older side, and in inverse grading the smaller grains are on the older side.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the order of events
paragraphs.text: A few principles help geologists set out the order in which events happened in a feature's geologic history. The Law of Superposition says younger rocks are laid down above older rocks, and stay that way as long as tectonic activity has not overturned the beds. The Law of Original Horizontality says beds are deposited horizontally because of gravity. Beds that are not horizontal have been tilted or warped by geologic processes. The law of Cross-Cutting Relationships says any feature that cuts through another is the younger of the two, and this can include a fault or an igneous dike cutting through sedimentary bedding.

paragraphs.heading: Why thickness and surfaces matter
paragraphs.text: Bed thickness is a basic and important characteristic. Analysing it can reveal breaks in sedimentation, cyclic patterns of sedimentation and gradual changes in the environment. Bedding also matters in geotechnical engineering. In tunnel, foundation or slope construction, a bedding surface often forms a discontinuity that may strongly affect the strength and deformation of soil and rock masses.
